newsitem.title: USA: General Signal sees earnings drop; stock falls.
newsitem.headline: General Signal sees earnings drop; stock falls.

text.p: General Signal Corp., a maker of industrial equipment, said Wednesday it expected lower earnings for the first quarter, disappointing investors and triggering a sell-off in its stock.
General Signal stock fell $3.25 to $40.375 after dipping as low as $38.50 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the most active issues.
The Stamford, Conn.-based company said it expects earnings before taxes and other items to fall about 7 percent in the first quarter because of lower orders, sales and cost pressures.
General Signal earned $25.4 million, or 51 cents a share, on revenues of $481.7 million in the 1996 quarter, including a gain equal to 1 cent a share from the sale of a business unit.
Analysts had forecast earnings of 53 cents a share on average for the 1997 quarter, according to the company.
General Signal attributed the shortfall to the company's businesses in fire systems, pumps and uninterruptible power supply equipment, which protect computers from power outages.
Despite the alarm bells over the first quarter, analysts said General Signal was on track to post solid full-year earnings growth.
They noted the company was expected to sell several of its 15 businesses, shore up distribution arrangements and expand in service and support, among other measures.
Analysts also pointed out that General Signal last year managed to deliver on full-year expectations despite a similar glitch in the first quarter.

"I don't think the outlook is all that grim," said Phua Young, an analyst at Lehman Brothers. "They're trying to reposition some businesses, they're coming out with some new products, and when you talk about trying to do all these things, you're not going to get smooth sailing."
Analysts said they were not veering from their full-year earnings estimates of $2.90 to $3.05 a share.
They said General Signal Chairman Michael Lockhart had a new team in place that was committed to turning the company around.

Analysts said Lockhart was focused on long-term growth and that he had a proven track record. Lockhart, formerly general manager of General Electric Co.'s Aircraft Engines business, joined General Signal in September 1994 and became chairman and chief executive officer in October 1995.

"Lockhart can improve profits because he is putting in place a lot of the regimes, such as reduction in working capital and cycle times, reducing product development times, and increasing customer service effectiveness," said Nick Heymann, analyst at NatWest Securities.
"He's also moving into expanding the after-market service and support business."

"Another catalyst for growth is the company's expected selling off of assets not strategic to the company and using the proceeds to repurchase stock," Heymann said. He declined to speculate on which assets would be sold.

"We definitely believe that this is one of the most misvalued stocks right now," said Heymann, adding that General Signal was well-positioned to improve profitability substantially by the end of 1998.
